lessons.title: Accounting concepts and the accounting equation

scenes.text: Ravi puts ₹1,00,000 of his savings into a new stationery shop and buys ₹30,000 of stock on credit.
His accountant friend shows him that every transaction keeps Assets = Liabilities + Capital in balance.

steps.title: Core concepts
steps.body:
- **Business entity**: the business is separate from its owner
- **Money measurement**: only events measurable in money are recorded
- **Going concern**: the business is assumed to continue
- **Accrual**: income and expenses recognised when earned/incurred, not when cash moves
- **Matching**: expenses matched with the revenue of the same period
- **Consistency**, **prudence (conservatism)**, **materiality**, **full disclosure**
- **Dual aspect**: every transaction has two equal effects ⇒ **Assets = Liabilities + Capital**

steps.title: Solved: transactions on the equation
steps.body:
1. Ravi starts with cash ₹1,00,000 → Assets 1,00,000 = Capital 1,00,000
2. Buys goods on credit ₹30,000 → Assets 1,30,000 = Creditors 30,000 + Capital 1,00,000
3. Sells goods costing ₹10,000 for ₹15,000 cash → Cash +15,000, Stock −10,000; profit 5,000 adds to capital

- Final: Assets 1,35,000 = Liabilities 30,000 + Capital **1,05,000** ✓

steps.title: Solved: drawings and expenses
steps.body:
Ravi pays rent ₹4,000 and withdraws ₹6,000 for personal use.

- Cash falls by 10,000 (assets 1,25,000)
- Capital falls by 4,000 (expense) and 6,000 (drawings) → 95,000
- 1,25,000 = 30,000 + 95,000 ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating owner's personal expenses as business expenses (violates entity concept).
- Recording only cash transactions (violates accrual).
- Thinking capital is cash — capital is the owner's claim on assets.
- Forgetting that profit increases capital.

activity.prompt: A business has assets ₹4,50,000 and liabilities ₹1,20,000. What is the owner's capital (₹)?

quiz.q: The concept that treats the business as separate from the owner:
quiz.why: The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner.
The accounting equation is A = L + C: assets equal liabilities plus capital.

quiz.q: Recording income when earned rather than received follows:
quiz.why: Recording income when it is earned, not when cash is received, follows the accrual concept.
Drawings are money or goods the owner takes for personal use. They reduce capital.

quiz.q: Providing for expected losses but not expected gains reflects:
quiz.why: Providing for expected losses but not expected gains is prudence (conservatism).

scenes.text: Meena runs a tailoring unit and keeps every bill in a shoebox. At year end, she has no idea who owes her what.
A journal records each transaction in date order; the ledger sorts them by account.

steps.title: Debit and credit rules
steps.body:
**Modern (accounting equation) approach**
- Assets, expenses, drawings: **debit** to increase, credit to decrease
- Liabilities, capital, revenue: **credit** to increase, debit to decrease

**Traditional golden rules**
- Personal accounts: debit the receiver, credit the giver
- Real accounts: debit what comes in, credit what goes out
- Nominal accounts: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains

steps.title: Solved: journal entries
steps.body:
- Paid rent ₹5,000: **Rent A/c Dr 5,000 / To Cash A/c 5,000**
- Bought machinery on credit from Sharma ₹50,000: **Machinery A/c Dr / To Sharma A/c**
- Goods withdrawn for personal use ₹2,000: **Drawings A/c Dr / To Purchases A/c**
- Received ₹9,800 from Gupta in full settlement of ₹10,000: **Cash Dr 9,800, Discount Allowed Dr 200 / To Gupta 10,000**

steps.title: Solved: posting and balancing
steps.body:
Cash account: Dr side — capital 1,00,000, sales 20,000; Cr side — rent 5,000, purchases 40,000.

- Total Dr 1,20,000; total Cr 45,000
- Balance c/d on the Cr side = **₹75,000 (debit balance)**, brought down on the Dr side next period.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting 'Goods' for drawings without using the Purchases account.
- Recording discount on the wrong side (discount allowed is an expense, Dr).
- Forgetting narration in journal entries.
- Confusing 'balance c/d' side with the type of balance.

activity.prompt: For each item, is the account debited or credited?

items.text: Cash when the owner introduces capital
Capital when the owner introduces cash

quiz.q: Purchase of furniture for cash: account debited:
quiz.why: Furniture is an asset. When an asset increases, it is debited, so debit Furniture and credit Cash.

quiz.q: Under golden rules, a personal account is debited when the person:
quiz.why: By the golden rule for personal accounts, debit the receiver and credit the giver. So a person who receives is debited.

quiz.q: Interest received is credited because it is:
quiz.why: Interest received is an income, a nominal account. By the rule 'credit all incomes and gains', it is credited.

quiz.q: Goods given as charity are credited to:
quiz.why: Goods given as charity reduce the goods available, so credit Purchases. The charity expense is debited.

quiz.q: A debit balance in a cash account means:
quiz.why: A debit balance in a cash account means receipts exceed payments, so there is cash in hand.

scenes.text: Arif's cash book says ₹20,000 in the bank; his passbook says ₹22,300.
Neither is wrong — some entries simply haven't reached the other record yet.

steps.title: Why the two differ
steps.body:
- Cheques **issued but not yet presented** (cash book reduced; bank not yet)
- Cheques **deposited but not yet cleared** (cash book increased; bank not yet)
- **Bank charges**, interest debited (bank first)
- **Interest credited**, direct deposits, dividends collected by bank (bank first)
- Errors by either party

Method: start with one balance; add items that make the other balance higher, subtract those that make it lower.

steps.title: Solved: starting from the cash book
steps.body:
Cash book (Dr) ₹20,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹5,000; deposited not cleared ₹3,000; bank charges ₹200; interest credited ₹500.

- 20,000 + 5,000 − 3,000 − 200 + 500
- Balance as per passbook = **₹22,300**

steps.title: Solved: overdraft
steps.body:
Overdraft as per cash book ₹10,000 (Cr). Cheques issued not presented ₹2,000; bank interest on overdraft ₹300 not in cash book.

- Treat overdraft as negative: −10,000 + 2,000 − 300 = −8,300
- Overdraft as per passbook = **₹8,300**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding when you should subtract — ask 'is the other record higher or lower because of this?'
- Forgetting that an overdraft reverses signs.
- Treating a dishonoured cheque as a deposit.
- Ignoring errors in the passbook (they also need adjustment).

activity.prompt: Passbook balance ₹15,000. Cheques deposited but not cleared ₹4,000; cheques issued not presented ₹6,000. What is the cash book balance (₹)?

quiz.why: A bank reconciliation statement is prepared by the account holder, to reconcile their cash book with the bank's passbook.

quiz.q: Cheques issued but not presented make passbook balance:
quiz.why: Cheques issued but not yet presented haven't been deducted by the bank. So the passbook balance is higher than the cash book balance.

quiz.q: Bank charges not yet in cash book make cash book balance:
quiz.why: If bank charges are not yet in the cash book, the bank has already deducted them. So the cash book balance is higher than the passbook.
If the bank collects a dividend directly, the passbook is credited first, so it shows a higher balance than the cash book.
A favourable balance in the passbook is a credit balance, because the bank owes that money to the customer.

lessons.title: Trial balance and rectification of errors

scenes.text: Sunita's trial balance shows debits ₹1,000 more than credits.
She parks the difference in a suspense account and hunts the error — the sales book was undercast.

steps.title: Trial balance and errors
steps.body:
A trial balance lists ledger balances; equal totals show **arithmetical accuracy**, not absence of all errors.

Errors that **do not** affect agreement:
- **Omission** (transaction not recorded)
- **Commission** (wrong account of the same class, e.g. Mohan instead of Sohan)
- **Principle** (capital vs revenue confusion)
- **Compensating** errors

Errors that **do** affect it: one-sided postings, wrong totals, wrong amounts on one side ⇒ use a **suspense account** until found.

steps.title: Solved: rectification entries
steps.body:
- Sales book undercast by ₹1,000: **Suspense A/c Dr 1,000 / To Sales A/c 1,000**
- Furniture ₹8,000 debited to Purchases (principle): **Furniture A/c Dr / To Purchases A/c 8,000** (no suspense)
- Credit sale to Mohan ₹3,000 posted to Sohan: **Mohan A/c Dr / To Sohan A/c 3,000**

steps.title: Solved: effect on profit
steps.body:
Repairs ₹2,000 wrongly debited to Machinery.

- Expense understated ⇒ profit **overstated by ₹2,000**
- Rectify: Repairs A/c Dr 2,000 / To Machinery A/c 2,000 (also check any depreciation charged on the extra 2,000)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using suspense for errors that don't affect the trial balance.
- Rectifying in the wrong direction (reverse the wrong effect, then record the right one).
- Believing an agreed trial balance proves the books are error-free.
- Forgetting the profit effect of capital/revenue errors.

activity.prompt: Does the error affect the agreement of the trial balance?

items.text: Wages for machine installation debited to Wages
Payment to Ram posted only to cash account
Sale to Hari posted to Harish's account
Discount allowed ₹50 posted to credit of discount account

quiz.why: An agreed trial balance proves arithmetical accuracy: total debits equal total credits. It doesn't prove there are no errors, since some errors don't affect it.

quiz.q: Wrong account of the same class is an error of:
quiz.why: Posting to a wrong account of the same class is an error of commission.

quiz.q: A suspense account is used for errors that:
quiz.why: A suspense account holds the difference in a trial balance caused by errors that affect it, until they are found.

quiz.q: Purchase of machinery debited to Purchases: profit is:
quiz.why: Debiting machinery (an asset) to Purchases (an expense) overstates expenses. So profit is understated.
An overcast sales book means sales were recorded ₹700 too high. To correct, debit Sales and credit Suspense.

questions.q: Capital = ₹2,00,000, liabilities = ₹50,000. Assets:
Salary paid is a ___ account:
questions.why: Salary paid is an expense, so it is a nominal account.

questions.q: A trial balance is prepared from:
questions.why: A trial balance is prepared from the balances of the ledger accounts.

questions.q: Bought goods from Lal on credit: credit:
questions.why: When goods are bought on credit from Lal, Lal is the giver of credit, so Lal's account is credited. Purchases is debited.

questions.q: Bank charges debited in passbook only. Starting from the cash book, to get passbook balance you:
questions.why: Bank charges debited only in the passbook have lowered the bank's balance, but the cash book hasn't recorded them yet. So starting from the cash book balance you subtract the charges to get the passbook balance.

questions.q: Error of omission affects the TB:
questions.why: An error of omission means a transaction was left out entirely, so both its debit and credit are missing. The trial balance still agrees, so it is not affected.

questions.q: Assertion: Matching principle requires depreciation to be charged. Reason: The asset helps earn revenue over its life.
questions.why: Under the matching principle, costs are matched with the revenue they help earn. An asset helps earn revenue over its life, so its cost is spread over periods as depreciation. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Cash book Dr ₹12,000; cheques deposited not cleared ₹2,500; interest credited by bank ₹300. Passbook balance:
questions.why: Cheques deposited but not yet cleared reduce the passbook balance, and interest credited by the bank increases it. So passbook balance = 12,000 − 2,500 + 300 = ₹9,800.

questions.q: Received ₹4,900 from a debtor in full settlement of ₹5,000. Entry includes:
questions.why: Cash received is ₹4,900 against ₹5,000 due, so ₹100 is discount allowed, which is an expense for the business. The entry debits Cash 4,900 and Discount allowed 100, and credits the debtor 5,000.

questions.q: Case: TB difference ₹600 (credit short) is put in suspense. Later found: purchases returns book undercast by ₹600. Rectification:
questions.why: The credit side was ₹600 short because the purchases returns book was undercast, so suspense was credited... To fix it, credit Purchase returns by 600 and clear the suspense account with a debit of 600.

questions.q: Overdraft as per passbook ₹5,000; cheques issued not presented ₹1,500. Overdraft as per cash book:
questions.why: Cheques issued but not presented haven't yet been deducted by the bank, so the passbook overdraft is smaller than the cash book's. The cash book overdraft = 5,000 + 1,500 = ₹6,500.

questions.q: Repairs ₹3,000 debited to Building; 10% depreciation charged on building. Net effect on profit before rectification:
questions.why: Repairs of ₹3,000 should be an expense, but it was capitalised, so profit is overstated by 3,000. Depreciation of 10% (₹300) was also charged on it, which understated profit by 300. Net overstatement = ₹2,700.

questions.q: Goods costing ₹8,000 sold at 25% profit on cost on credit; equation change:
questions.why: Selling goods costing ₹8,000 at 25% profit on cost gives a price of ₹10,000. Debtors rise by 10,000 and stock falls by 8,000, so net assets rise by 2,000, which is the profit added to capital.

questions.q: Sales ₹1,500 to Kiran was correctly entered in the sales book but posted to Kiran's account as ₹5,100. Rectification:
questions.why: The sales book was right at ₹1,500, but Kiran was debited ₹5,100, which is ₹3,600 too much. To fix, credit Kiran by 3,600 and debit Suspense 3,600, which held the difference.

questions.q: Which error is NOT revealed by a trial balance?
questions.why: Compensating errors of equal amounts on opposite sides cancel each other out, so the trial balance still agrees. The other errors would make it disagree.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Depreciation by straight-line and written-down-value methods, provisions and reserves, final accounts with adjustments, and partnership basics including appropriation and goodwill.
outcomes: Learners can compute depreciation and profit or loss on sale
Learners can create provisions for doubtful debts
Learners can prepare trading, P&L and balance sheet with adjustments
Learners can prepare a profit and loss appropriation account and value goodwill

scenes.text: A bakery buys a van for ₹10,00,000. It will serve for years, so its cost shouldn't hit one year's profit alone.
Depreciation spreads the cost over the van's useful life.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
Depreciation is the systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount (cost − residual value) over its useful life (guided by Ind AS 16 / AS 10 and, for companies, Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013).

- **Straight-line (SLM)**: annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value)/Useful life — same every year
- **Written-down value (WDV)**: fixed % on the opening book value — falls each year
- Cost includes purchase price + installation + freight etc. needed to bring the asset to use

steps.title: Solved: SLM and sale
steps.body:
Machine cost ₹1,00,000 + installation ₹10,000; residual ₹10,000; life 5 years.

- Annual depreciation = (1,10,000 − 10,000)/5 = **₹20,000**
- Sold after 3 years for ₹45,000: book value = 1,10,000 − 60,000 = 50,000 ⇒ **loss ₹5,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving installation or freight out of cost.
- Applying the WDV rate to original cost every year.
- Forgetting time-proportion depreciation for assets bought mid-year.
- Treating depreciation as a cash outflow (it is non-cash).

activity.prompt: An asset costs ₹2,00,000 and is depreciated at 10% WDV. What is its book value at the end of year 2 (₹)?

quiz.why: Under the straight-line method (SLM), the same fixed amount of depreciation is charged every year.

quiz.q: Installation charges on a machine are:
quiz.why: Installation charges are needed to bring a machine into use, so they are added to its cost. They are capital expenditure, not an expense.

quiz.q: Under WDV, the asset value never reaches:
quiz.why: Under the WDV method, depreciation is a percentage of the declining balance, so the asset value gets smaller each year but never reaches zero.
Depreciation is a non-cash expense. It spreads the cost of an asset over its life, with no cash going out in the year.

quiz.q: Machine ₹60,000, residual ₹0, life 6 years, bought 1 October, year ending 31 March. First year SLM depreciation:
quiz.why: Annual SLM depreciation = 60,000 ÷ 6 = ₹10,000. The machine was used from 1 October to 31 March, 6 months, so the first-year charge is 10,000 × 6/12 = ₹5,000.

scenes.text: A wholesaler has ₹50,000 owed by retailers. Experience says about 5% will never pay.
Prudence says: provide for that loss now.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Bad debts**: definitely irrecoverable — written off to P&L
- **Provision for doubtful debts**: estimated future loss on remaining debtors; a **charge against profit**
- **Reserve**: an **appropriation of profit** (general reserve, capital reserve from capital profits, secret reserve)
- Provision for discount on debtors is calculated after deducting bad debts and the doubtful-debt provision

steps.title: Solved: provision
steps.body:
Debtors ₹50,000; further bad debts ₹2,000; create 5% provision.

- Good debtors = 48,000; provision = **₹2,400**
- P&L charge = 2,000 + 2,400 (if no old provision) = **₹4,400**
- Balance sheet: Debtors 48,000 − 2,400 = **₹45,600**

steps.title: Solved: existing provision
steps.body:
Old provision ₹3,000. Bad debts ₹1,000. New provision required ₹2,400.

- Needed = 1,000 + 2,400 = 3,400; available 3,000
- Extra P&L charge = **₹400**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating the provision before deducting further bad debts.
- Treating reserves as charges against profit.
- Showing provisions on the liabilities side without deducting from debtors (modern format deducts).
- Double-counting bad debts already in the trial balance.

statements.s: A provision is a charge against profit.
A reserve is created before calculating net profit.
statements.why: It is an appropriation of profit.

statements.s: Provision for doubtful debts follows the prudence concept.
Capital reserve is usually created from capital profits.
statements.why: E.g. profit on sale of fixed assets or prior to incorporation.

quiz.why: Bad debts are a loss, so they are debited to the Profit and Loss account.
Provision is on debtors after deducting bad debts: 80,000 − 4,000 = 76,000. 5% of 76,000 = ₹3,800.
A general reserve is an appropriation of profit: money set aside from profits. It's not a charge against profit, like a provision.

quiz.q: Old provision ₹5,000; bad debts ₹2,000; new provision ₹4,000. P&L charge:
quiz.why: The P&L charge = bad debts + new provision − old provision = 2,000 + 4,000 − 5,000 = ₹1,000.

quiz.q: Secret reserves are found mainly in:
quiz.why: Secret reserves were historically found in banks and insurance companies, created by understating assets or overstating liabilities. Today they are restricted.

scenes.text: On 31 March, Lakshmi counts her stock, notes unpaid salaries and rent paid in advance.
These adjustments turn a raw trial balance into true and fair final accounts.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Trading A/c**: Opening stock + Purchases (− returns) + Direct expenses vs Sales (− returns) + Closing stock ⇒ **Gross profit**
- **Profit & Loss A/c**: GP + other incomes − indirect expenses (salaries, rent, depreciation, bad debts…) ⇒ **Net profit**
- **Balance sheet**: assets and liabilities at year end; net profit added to capital, drawings deducted

Each adjustment appears **twice**: e.g. outstanding salary → add to salary in P&L and show as a liability.

steps.title: Solved: net profit with adjustments
steps.body:
From GP 40,000: salaries 12,000 (₹1,000 outstanding); rent 6,000 (₹1,000 prepaid); depreciation 2,000.

- Salaries 13,000; rent 5,000; depreciation 2,000
- NP = 40,000 − 20,000 = **₹20,000**
- Balance sheet: outstanding salary 1,000 (liability), prepaid rent 1,000 (asset)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recording an adjustment only once.
- Putting closing stock inside the trial balance and in the trading account again (only if it is not already in the TB).
- Classifying carriage outwards as a direct expense (it is selling, P&L).
- Forgetting to deduct drawings from capital.

activity.prompt: Where does each item go?

quiz.why: Outstanding wages are wages owed but not yet paid. They are added to wages in the P&L and shown as a liability in the balance sheet.
Prepaid insurance is paid in advance, so its benefit is still to be received. It is shown as a current asset.

quiz.q: Closing stock (not in TB) appears in:
options: Trading A/c credit and balance sheet
quiz.why: Closing stock given outside the trial balance appears on the credit side of the Trading account, and as a current asset in the balance sheet.

options: added to income and shown as asset
quiz.why: Accrued interest on investments is earned but not yet received. It is added to income and shown as an asset (accrued income).

scenes.text: Asha, Bilal and Charu start a café without a written deed. A year later they argue over salary and interest.
The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 gives default rules — and good firms write a clear deed.

steps.title: Default rules (no agreement)
steps.body:
Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, unless the partners agree otherwise:
- Profits and losses shared **equally**
- **No interest on capital**; no interest on drawings
- **No salary** or commission to partners
- Interest on a partner's **loan** to the firm at **6% p.a.**

The **P&L Appropriation A/c** distributes net profit: interest on capital, salaries, commission, then the balance in the profit-sharing ratio.

steps.title: Solved: goodwill by super profit
steps.body:
Average profit ₹60,000; capital employed ₹4,00,000; normal rate 10%.

- Normal profit = 40,000; super profit = 20,000
- Goodwill at 3 years' purchase = **₹60,000**
- Capitalisation of super profit at 10% = 20,000/0.10 = ₹2,00,000 (another method)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving interest on capital when the deed is silent.
- Charging interest on a partner's loan in the appropriation account (it is a charge against profit in P&L).
- Using total profit instead of super profit for 'years' purchase of super profit'.
- Forgetting that the deed overrides the default rules.

activity.prompt: X and Y share profits 2 : 1. Net profit ₹90,000; X gets salary ₹15,000 and no interest on capital is allowed. What is Y's share of the remaining profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Without a deed, interest on a partner's loan is:
quiz.why: Without a partnership deed, a partner's loan to the firm earns interest at 6% per annum, under the Partnership Act.

quiz.q: Without a deed, profits are shared:
quiz.why: Without a partnership deed, profits and losses are shared equally among partners.
Partners' salaries are an appropriation of profit, so they are debited to the P&L Appropriation account, not the P&L account.
Super profit = actual (average) profit − normal profit. It is the excess over normal profit.

quiz.q: Average profit 50,000; normal profit 30,000; 2 years' purchase of super profit:
quiz.why: Super profit = 50,000 − 30,000 = 20,000. With 2 years' purchase, goodwill = 20,000 × 2 = ₹40,000.

questions.q: Depreciation is charged on:
questions.why: Depreciation is charged on fixed (non-current) assets, since they are used over many years. Current assets and liabilities are not depreciated.

questions.q: Gross profit is found in the:
questions.why: Gross profit is found in the Trading account. Net profit is found in the P&L account.

questions.q: Partnership in India is governed by the:
questions.why: Partnerships in India are governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

questions.q: SLM: cost ₹50,000, residual ₹5,000, life 9 years. Annual depreciation:
questions.why: SLM depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ life = (50,000 − 5,000) ÷ 9 = ₹5,000.

questions.q: Unpaid rent at year end is a:
questions.why: Unpaid rent at year end is an outstanding expense. It is a current liability.

questions.q: Provision for doubtful debts is deducted from:
questions.why: A provision for doubtful debts is deducted from debtors in the balance sheet, showing net debtors.

questions.q: Assertion: Interest on partners' capital is allowed only if the deed provides. Reason: The Partnership Act allows no interest on capital by default.
questions.why: Under the Partnership Act, no interest on capital is allowed unless the deed provides for it. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: WDV 15% on ₹4,00,000. Depreciation in year 2:
Opening stock 20,000; purchases 80,000; sales 1,20,000; closing stock 25,000; carriage inwards 5,000. Gross profit:
questions.why: Cost of goods sold = 20,000 + 80,000 + 5,000 − 25,000 = 80,000. Gross profit = 1,20,000 − 80,000 = ₹40,000. Carriage inwards is part of the cost of goods.

questions.q: Case: Debtors ₹1,20,000; bad debts ₹5,000; provision 4%; old provision ₹3,000. P&L charge for bad and doubtful debts:
questions.why: Provision = 4% of (1,20,000 − 5,000) = 4,600. The charge = bad debts 5,000 + new provision 4,600 − old provision 3,000 = ₹6,600.

questions.q: Machine bought 1 April for ₹1,20,000 (SLM 10% on cost). Sold 1 October of year 3 for ₹90,000. Profit/loss:
questions.why: Depreciation for 2.5 years × ₹12,000 = ₹30,000 ⇒ book value ₹90,000 = sale price.

questions.q: P and Q share 3 : 2; P's capital ₹3,00,000, Q's ₹2,00,000; interest on capital 5%; profit before interest ₹15,000. Under the deed (interest only out of profits), P receives:
questions.why: Interest 15,000 + 10,000 = 25,000 > profit ⇒ profit shared in interest ratio 3 : 2.

questions.q: A firm earns ₹90,000 on capital ₹6,00,000; normal rate 12%. Goodwill by capitalising super profit:
Insurance ₹12,000 paid on 1 July for one year; year ends 31 March. Prepaid amount:
questions.why: The ₹12,000 insurance covers 1 July to 30 June. By 31 March, 9 months are used, so 3 months (April–June) are prepaid: 12,000 × 3/12 = ₹3,000.

questions.q: Under the matching concept, an expense whose benefit extends to next year should be:
questions.why: Under the matching concept, the part of an expense that benefits the next year is carried forward as a prepaid expense, and only the used part is charged now.

courses.summary: Cost concepts and classification, the cost sheet, material control (EOQ, stock levels, pricing of issues) and labour and overhead costing (incentives, absorption).
outcomes: Learners can classify costs and split semi-variable costs
Learners can prepare a cost sheet
Learners can compute EOQ, stock levels and issue prices
Learners can apply Halsey and Rowan plans and overhead rates

scenes.text: A garment unit owner knows total monthly costs but not the cost of one shirt.
Classifying costs — direct or indirect, fixed or variable — is the first step.

steps.title: Classifications
steps.body:
- **By element**: material, labour, expenses (each direct or indirect)
- **By behaviour**: fixed (rent), variable (raw material), semi-variable (electricity with a fixed charge)
- **By function**: production, administration, selling and distribution
- **For decisions**: sunk (already incurred, irrelevant), opportunity (benefit forgone), marginal, relevant
- **Cost unit** (per tonne, per kWh, per passenger-km) and **cost centre** (department/machine)

steps.title: Solved: per-unit behaviour
steps.body:
Fixed cost ₹1,00,000.

- At 10,000 units: ₹10 per unit; at 20,000 units: ₹5 per unit
- Variable cost per unit stays the same (say ₹8); total variable cost doubles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fixed cost per unit is constant (it falls as output rises).
- Including sunk costs in decisions.
- Treating all indirect costs as fixed.
- Mixing up cost unit and cost centre.

activity.prompt: Classify by behaviour.

quiz.q: A cost already incurred that cannot be changed:
quiz.why: A sunk cost has already been incurred and can't be changed by any future decision. So it is irrelevant for decisions.

quiz.q: Fixed cost per unit as output rises:
quiz.why: Fixed cost per unit falls as output rises, because the same total fixed cost is spread over more units.

quiz.q: Cost unit for a power plant:
quiz.why: The cost unit for a power plant is per kWh, which is its measure of output.

quiz.q: Direct material + direct labour + direct expenses =
quiz.why: Direct material + direct labour + direct expenses = prime cost.
By the high–low method, variable cost per unit = change in cost ÷ change in units = (18,000 − 14,000) ÷ (3,000 − 2,000) = ₹4.

scenes.text: A furniture firm must quote for 500 school desks.
A cost sheet built up layer by layer gives the cost per desk and a fair quote.

steps.title: Layers of cost
steps.body:
- **Prime cost** = direct material + direct labour + direct expenses
- **Works (factory) cost** = prime cost + factory overheads (+ opening WIP − closing WIP)
- **Cost of production** = works cost + office & administration overheads
- **Cost of goods sold** = cost of production + opening finished goods − closing finished goods
- **Cost of sales** = COGS + selling & distribution overheads
- **Profit** = sales − cost of sales

steps.title: Solved: a complete cost sheet
steps.body:
DM 40,000; DL 25,000; DE 5,000; factory OH 15,000; office OH 10,000; S&D 8,000; sales 1,25,000; 1,000 units, no stocks.

- Prime cost 70,000 → works cost 85,000 → cost of production 95,000
- Cost of sales **1,03,000** (₹103 per unit)
- Profit **22,000** (₹22 per unit)

steps.title: Solved: quoting a price
steps.body:
Same firm wants a 20% profit on sales for an order of 200 units.

- Cost of sales per unit ₹103
- Price = 103/(1 − 0.20) = **₹128.75 per unit**
- (20% on cost would instead give ₹123.60 — read the question carefully.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding selling overheads before cost of production.
- Forgetting WIP adjustments in works cost.
- Confusing profit on cost with profit on sales.
- Including interest, dividends or income tax in cost (these are financial items).

activity.prompt: Order the layers of a cost sheet.
items: Prime cost
Works (factory) cost
Cost of production
Cost of goods sold
Cost of sales
Profit

quiz.why: Factory overheads are added to prime cost to get works (factory) cost.
Selling overheads are added at the last stage, to cost of production, so they appear in the cost of sales.

quiz.q: Cost of sales ₹80; profit 20% on sales. Selling price:
quiz.why: A profit of 20% on sales means cost is 80% of the selling price. So price = 80 ÷ 0.8 = ₹100.

quiz.q: Which is excluded from a cost sheet?
quiz.why: Income tax is an appropriation of profit, not a cost of production, so it is excluded from a cost sheet.

quiz.q: Prime cost 50,000; factory OH 10,000; opening WIP 5,000; closing WIP 8,000. Works cost:
quiz.why: Works cost = prime cost + factory overhead + opening WIP − closing WIP = 50,000 + 10,000 + 5,000 − 8,000 = ₹57,000.

lessons.title: Material control: EOQ, stock levels, pricing issues

story.title: Too much cement, too little steel

scenes.text: A builder's yard overflows with cement while work stops for lack of steel.
Material control sets how much to order and when — EOQ and stock levels.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **EOQ** = √(2AO/C): A = annual usage, O = ordering cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year
- **Re-order level** = maximum usage × maximum lead time
- **Minimum level** = ROL − (normal usage × normal lead time)
- **Maximum level** = ROL + ROQ − (minimum usage × minimum lead time)
- **Average stock** ≈ (min + max)/2 or min + ½ROQ
- **ABC analysis**: A items (few, high value) controlled tightly; C items (many, low value) loosely
- Pricing issues: FIFO, LIFO (not permitted under Ind AS for inventory valuation), weighted average

steps.title: Solved: EOQ
steps.body:
A = 4,800 units/yr, O = ₹150/order, C = ₹4/unit/yr.

- EOQ = √(2 × 4,800 × 150/4) = √3,60,000 = **600 units**
- Orders per year = 8; at EOQ, annual ordering cost = carrying cost = ₹1,200

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using monthly usage with annual carrying cost in EOQ.
- Mixing normal and maximum figures in stock-level formulas.
- Forgetting carrying cost can be given as % of unit price (C = rate × price).
- Applying LIFO for financial-statement inventory under Ind AS.

activity.prompt: Annual demand 7,200 units, ordering cost ₹50 per order, carrying cost 20% of unit price ₹10. What is the EOQ (units)?

quiz.why: At EOQ, ordering cost equals carrying cost, which makes total inventory cost the minimum.
Re-order level = maximum usage × maximum lead time, so that stock-outs are avoided.

quiz.q: ABC analysis gives tightest control to:
quiz.why: In ABC analysis, 'A' items are few but high in value, so they get the tightest control.

quiz.q: In rising prices, FIFO charges production with:
quiz.why: In FIFO, the oldest stock is issued first. In rising prices, production is charged with older, lower prices.

scenes.text: A worker finishes a 10-hour job in 8 hours. How much bonus is fair?
Halsey and Rowan plans share the time saved between worker and employer.

steps.title: Labour
steps.body:
- **Labour turnover (separation method)** = separations/average number of workers × 100
- **Halsey**: wages = (time taken × rate) + 50% × time saved × rate
- **Rowan**: wages = (time taken × rate) + (time saved/time allowed) × time taken × rate
- Idle time (normal vs abnormal) and overtime premium treatment

steps.title: Overheads
steps.body:
- Allocation (whole item to one centre) vs apportionment (shared on a fair basis: floor area for rent, HP × hours for power)
- Service department costs re-apportioned to production departments
- **Absorption rates**: machine hour rate, labour hour rate, % of prime cost
- Under-/over-absorption = absorbed − actual; usually written off to costing P&L

steps.title: Solved: Halsey vs Rowan
steps.body:
Time allowed 10 h, taken 8 h, rate ₹50/h.

- Basic = 8 × 50 = 400
- Halsey bonus = 50% × 2 × 50 = 50 ⇒ **₹450**
- Rowan bonus = (2/10) × 8 × 50 = 80 ⇒ **₹480**

steps.title: Solved: machine hour rate and absorption
steps.body:
Budgeted overheads ₹1,20,000; machine hours 6,000.

- MHR = **₹20/hour**
- Actual hours 6,300, actual overheads ₹1,30,000 ⇒ absorbed 1,26,000 ⇒ **under-absorbed ₹4,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using time allowed instead of time taken for basic pay.
- Forgetting Rowan's bonus can never exceed the basic wage.
- Apportioning rent by number of workers instead of floor area.
- Calling over-absorption a loss.

activity.prompt: Time allowed 20 h, time taken 15 h, rate ₹40/h. Total wages under the Rowan plan (₹)?

quiz.why: In the Halsey plan, the worker gets a bonus of 50% of the time saved × the hourly rate.

quiz.q: Rent of a factory is apportioned on:
quiz.why: Factory rent is apportioned on the basis of floor area, since that is what the space each department uses.
Absorbed overhead is ₹50,000 and actual is ₹46,000. Absorbed more than actual is over-absorption of ₹4,000.
Average workers = (180 + 220) ÷ 2 = 200. Turnover = separations ÷ average workers = 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = 10%.

quiz.q: Power costs are often apportioned on:
quiz.why: Power costs are apportioned on HP × machine hours, since that shows how much power each machine uses.

questions.q: Prime cost includes:
questions.why: Prime cost includes direct costs only: direct material, direct labour and direct expenses.

questions.q: Cost that changes in total with output:
questions.why: A variable cost changes in total with the level of output.

questions.q: EOQ balances:
questions.why: EOQ balances ordering costs and carrying costs, giving the lowest total cost.

questions.q: Office salaries belong to:
questions.why: Office salaries are administration overheads.

questions.q: Maximum level is reduced by:
questions.why: Minimum level = re-order level − (normal usage × normal lead time). Of the options, min usage × min lead time is used in the maximum level formula, where it is subtracted.

questions.q: Halsey wage for 6 h taken, 8 h allowed, ₹30/h:
questions.why: Halsey wage = 6 h × ₹30 = 180, plus 50% of the 2 h saved × ₹30 = 30. Total = ₹210.

questions.q: Assertion: Sunk costs are irrelevant for decisions. Reason: They cannot be changed by any future action.
questions.why: A sunk cost can't be changed by any future action, so it is irrelevant. Only future differential costs matter. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Cost of production ₹2,00,000; opening FG ₹20,000; closing FG ₹30,000; S&D ₹15,000. Cost of sales:
questions.why: Cost of goods sold = 2,00,000 + 20,000 (opening FG) − 30,000 (closing FG) = ₹1,90,000. Adding selling and distribution overheads of ₹15,000 gives a cost of sales of ₹2,05,000.

questions.q: Opening 200 @ ₹5; purchases 300 @ ₹6; issue 400 (FIFO). Value of issue:
questions.why: By FIFO, the 400 units issued are the 200 opening at ₹5 (₹1,000) and 200 from purchases at ₹6 (₹1,200). Total = ₹2,200.

questions.q: Case: Max usage 300/day, lead time 10–15 days, normal usage 250, normal lead 12 days. ROL and minimum level:
questions.why: ROL = max usage × max lead time = 300 × 15 = 4,500. Minimum level = ROL − (normal usage × normal lead time) = 4,500 − (250 × 12) = 1,500.

questions.q: Rowan wages: allowed 12 h, taken 9 h, ₹60/h:
questions.why: Rowan wages = time taken × rate + (time saved ÷ time allowed) × time taken × rate = 9 × 60 + (3/12) × 9 × 60 = 540 + 135 = ₹675.

questions.q: High–low: March 4,000 units ₹30,000; June 6,000 units ₹40,000. Cost at 7,000 units:
Annual demand 12,000; ordering cost ₹60; price ₹20; carrying 15% of price. EOQ:
Overheads absorbed at ₹25/MH. Actual overheads ₹2,40,000; actual MH 9,000. Result:
questions.why: Overheads absorbed = 9,000 MH × ₹25 = ₹2,25,000. Actual overheads are ₹2,40,000, so ₹15,000 is under-absorbed.

questions.q: Under Rowan, as time taken approaches 50% of time allowed, bonus as % of basic wage approaches:
questions.why: Under Rowan, bonus as a percentage of basic wages equals time saved ÷ time allowed. When the time taken is 50% of the time allowed, that is 50%.

courses.title: Cost Accounting II · marginal costing, decisions, variances, budgets
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Marginal costing and cost–volume–profit analysis, decisions using contribution (key factor, make or buy, special orders), standard costing variances for material and labour, and flexible budgets.
outcomes: Learners can compute break-even, P/V ratio and margin of safety
Learners can rank products by contribution per key factor
Learners can compute and reconcile material and labour variances
Learners can flex a budget to a new activity level

story.title: How many cups to break even?

scenes.text: A college café sells bubble tea at ₹50; ingredients cost ₹30 a cup; rent and salaries are ₹2,00,000 a year.
How many cups before it makes any profit? CVP analysis answers in one line.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Contribution** = sales − variable cost; per unit = SP − VC
- **P/V ratio** = contribution/sales × 100
- **Break-even point (units)** = fixed cost/contribution per unit
- **BEP (₹)** = fixed cost/P/V ratio
- **Margin of safety** = actual sales − BE sales; profit = MOS × P/V ratio
- Sales for target profit = (FC + target profit)/P/V ratio
- P/V ratio from two periods = Δprofit/Δsales

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing fixed cost by selling price instead of contribution.
- Using P/V ratio as a decimal in one place and a percentage in another.
- Treating fixed costs as varying with output in short-run CVP.
- Forgetting that a price cut lowers contribution per unit and raises BEP.

activity.prompt: Fixed cost ₹3,00,000; selling price ₹100; variable cost ₹60. How many units must be sold for a profit of ₹1,00,000?

quiz.why: P/V ratio = contribution ÷ sales.
At break-even, profit is zero, so contribution just equals fixed cost.
Profit = margin of safety × P/V ratio = 2,00,000 × 25% = ₹50,000.

quiz.q: If variable cost per unit rises, BEP:
quiz.why: If variable cost per unit rises, contribution per unit falls. So more units are needed to cover fixed costs, and the BEP rises.
BEP sales = fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio = 60,000 ÷ 0.4 = ₹1,50,000.

scenes.text: A workshop makes two products but steel is rationed to 2,000 kg a month.
Which product deserves the steel? The one with the highest contribution per kg.

steps.title: Decision rules
steps.body:
- Fixed costs that don't change are **irrelevant**; compare **contribution** (or differential cost)
- **Key (limiting) factor**: rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource
- **Make or buy**: buy if purchase price < variable cost of making (+ any avoidable fixed cost)
- **Special order** with spare capacity: accept if price > variable cost (and no harm to regular sales)
- **Shut down/drop a product**: keep if it makes a positive contribution towards fixed costs (unless the capacity has a better use)

steps.title: Solved: key factor
steps.body:
X: contribution ₹40/unit, 4 kg steel. Y: ₹30/unit, 2 kg.

- Per kg: X = 10, Y = **15**
- With 2,000 kg and demand for Y of 600 units: make 600 Y (1,200 kg), then 200 X (800 kg)
- Total contribution = 18,000 + 8,000 = **₹26,000**

steps.title: Solved: make or buy
steps.body:
Making a part: material 20, labour 10, variable OH 5, apportioned fixed OH 8 (unavoidable). Supplier price ₹38.

- Relevant cost of making = 35 < 38 ⇒ **make** (saves ₹3/unit)
- If ₹8 fixed OH were avoidable, cost would be 43 ⇒ buy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ranking by contribution per unit instead of per unit of key factor.
- Including unavoidable fixed costs in make-or-buy.
- Accepting a special order below variable cost.
- Dropping a product that covers part of fixed costs without an alternative.

a.text: A factory with spare capacity gets a one-off order for 1,000 units at ₹35. Variable cost ₹30; full cost incl. fixed overheads ₹40. Accept?

choices.label: Accept — it adds ₹5,000 contribution
choices.feedback: Right: fixed costs are already covered and don't change.

choices.label: Reject — price is below full cost
choices.feedback: Full cost includes fixed costs that won't change.

a2.text: Think about which costs actually change if you accept.

b.text: Would your answer change if accepting meant cutting regular sales at ₹50?

choices.label: Yes — lost contribution of ₹20/unit outweighs ₹5 gain
No — still accept
choices.feedback: You'd lose more than you gain.

b2.text: Compare ₹5 gained with ₹20 lost per displaced regular unit.

end.text: Relevant costing: include only future costs and benefits that differ between options.

quiz.q: With a key factor, rank by:
quiz.why: When a key (limiting) factor exists, rank products by contribution per unit of the key factor, not per unit of product.
Unavoidable fixed costs remain whether you make or buy, so they are irrelevant to the decision.

quiz.q: Special order with spare capacity: minimum price:
quiz.why: With spare capacity, fixed costs are already covered. So the minimum price for a special order is the variable cost, plus any extra cost it causes.

quiz.q: A product with negative contribution should usually be:
quiz.why: A product with negative contribution makes the firm worse off with each unit sold, so it should usually be dropped.

quiz.q: A: contribution ₹60, 3 machine hours; B: ₹40, 1 hour. Hours scarce; prefer:
quiz.why: Contribution per machine hour: A = 60 ÷ 3 = ₹20, B = 40 ÷ 1 = ₹40. With hours scarce, prefer B.

lessons.title: Standard costing: material and labour variances

story.title: Why did the cake cost more?

scenes.text: A bakery's standard says each batch needs 10 kg of flour at ₹5/kg. This month a batch used 12 kg at ₹4.50.
Variances split the overspend: cheaper flour (good) but more of it (bad).

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
(SQ standard quantity for actual output, AQ actual quantity, SP standard price, AP actual price; similarly SH/AH and SR/AR for labour.)

- **Material cost variance** = SQ × SP − AQ × AP
- **Material price variance** = (SP − AP) × AQ
- **Material usage variance** = (SQ − AQ) × SP
- **Labour cost variance** = SH × SR − AH × AR
- **Labour rate variance** = (SR − AR) × AH
- **Labour efficiency variance** = (SH − AH) × SR
- Positive = Favourable (F), negative = Adverse (A); components add up to the total

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using budgeted quantity instead of standard quantity for actual output.
- Multiplying price variance by SQ instead of AQ.
- Labelling signs wrongly (actual cost higher = adverse).
- Not reconciling sub-variances to the total.

activity.prompt: Standard: 2 kg @ ₹10 per unit. Actual output 500 units used 1,100 kg @ ₹9.50. What is the material usage variance in ₹ (enter negative for adverse)?

quiz.why: Material price variance = (standard price − actual price) × actual quantity. It uses the actual quantity bought.
Labour efficiency variance = (standard hours − actual hours) × standard rate. It uses the standard rate.

quiz.q: Actual cost lower than standard cost gives:
quiz.why: When actual cost is lower than standard cost, the variance is favourable (a saving).

quiz.q: MPV ₹300 F and MUV ₹500 A. MCV:
quiz.why: Material cost variance = price variance + usage variance = 300 F − 500 A = ₹200 A.

quiz.q: A cheaper, lower-quality material often causes:
quiz.why: A cheaper, lower-quality material gives a favourable price variance, but more wastage causes an adverse usage variance.

scenes.text: A manager is blamed for spending ₹20,000 over budget — but output was 20% higher than planned.
A flexible budget compares like with like: what costs should have been at the actual output.

steps.title: Types of budgets
steps.body:
- **Functional budgets**: sales (usually the key budget), production, materials, labour, overheads, cash
- **Master budget**: summary budgeted P&L and balance sheet
- **Fixed budget**: one activity level; **flexible budget**: adjusts to actual activity using cost behaviour
- **Zero-based budgeting**: every expense justified afresh each period
- **Cash budget**: receipts and payments by month to spot shortfalls
- Budgetary control: set budgets → record actuals → compare → act on variances

steps.title: Solved: flexing a budget
steps.body:
At 10,000 units: VC ₹6/unit; FC ₹40,000; semi-variable ₹20,000 (50% fixed). Flex to 12,000 units.

- Variable: 12,000 × 6 = 72,000
- Fixed: 40,000
- Semi-variable: fixed 10,000 + variable (10,000/10,000 = ₹1/unit) × 12,000 = 22,000
- Total = **₹1,34,000** (vs ₹1,20,000 at 10,000 units)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing actual costs with a fixed budget at a different activity level.
- Flexing fixed costs.
- Recording credit sales as cash in the month of sale.
- Including depreciation in a cash budget (non-cash).

activity.prompt: Order the budgetary control cycle.
items: Set objectives and the key (limiting) factor
Prepare functional budgets
Combine into the master budget
Record actual results
Compare actual with flexed budget and analyse variances
Take corrective action and revise plans

quiz.why: A flexible budget is adjusted to the actual level of activity, so costs are compared like for like.
Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so it is excluded from a cash budget.
The sales budget is usually prepared first, because sales is often the key factor on which the other budgets depend.
Zero-based budgeting requires every expense to be justified from zero, not just based on last year's figures.

quiz.q: Fixed costs in a flexible budget:
quiz.why: In a flexible budget, fixed costs stay the same in total within the relevant range of activity. Only variable costs change.

questions.q: Contribution =
questions.why: Contribution = sales − variable cost.

questions.q: At BEP, profit is:
questions.why: At the break-even point, there's no profit and no loss, so profit is zero.

questions.q: A favourable variance means actual cost is:
questions.why: A favourable variance means actual cost is lower than the standard cost.

questions.q: SP ₹80, VC ₹50, FC ₹90,000. BEP units:
questions.why: Contribution per unit = 80 − 50 = ₹30. BEP = 90,000 ÷ 30 = 3,000 units.

questions.q: P/V ratio if SP ₹200, VC ₹120:
Standard 5 h @ ₹30; actual 6 h @ ₹30. Labour efficiency variance:
questions.why: Labour efficiency variance = (5 − 6) × 30 = ₹30 adverse, since more hours were used than the standard.

questions.q: Assertion: A flexible budget is better for control than a fixed budget when activity varies. Reason: It shows allowable costs at the actual level of activity.
questions.why: A flexible budget shows allowable costs at the actual activity level, so it gives a like-for-like comparison. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Sales ₹6,00,000; BEP sales ₹4,50,000; P/V 30%. Profit:
Material: SQ 400 kg @ ₹8; AQ 420 kg @ ₹7.50. MPV:
questions.why: MPV = (SP − AP) × AQ = (8 − 7.50) × 420 = ₹210, favourable because the actual price is lower.

questions.q: Case: Two years — sales ₹2,00,000 profit ₹20,000; sales ₹3,00,000 profit ₹50,000. Fixed cost:
questions.why: P/V = change in profit ÷ change in sales = 30,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 30%. At 2,00,000 sales, contribution = 60,000, so fixed cost = 60,000 − 20,000 = ₹40,000.

questions.q: A part costs ₹50 to make (VC ₹42, unavoidable FC ₹8). Supplier quotes ₹45. Decision:
questions.why: For a make-or-buy decision, only relevant costs count. The unavoidable fixed cost of ₹8 is irrelevant, so making costs ₹42 against ₹45 to buy. So make it.

questions.q: Labour: SH 200 @ ₹15; AH 190 @ ₹16. LRV and LEV:
questions.why: LRV = (SR − AR) × AH = (15 − 16) × 190 = ₹190 adverse. LEV = (SH − AH) × SR = (200 − 190) × 15 = ₹150 favourable.

questions.q: FC ₹1,20,000; SP ₹60; VC ₹36. If SP falls 10%, new BEP units:
questions.why: If SP falls 10%, it is ₹54 and contribution = 54 − 36 = ₹18. New BEP = 1,20,000 ÷ 18 ≈ 6,667 units.

questions.q: Products A (₹24 contribution, 3 labour hours) and B (₹20, 2 h). 700 hours available; max demand 200 of each. Optimal contribution:
questions.why: Per hour: B ₹10, A ₹8 ⇒ make 200 B (400 h, ₹4,000), then 100 A with the remaining 300 h (₹2,400).

scenes.text: In accounts papers, presentation earns marks. Kunal practises formats until they're automatic.
Then he only has to think about the numbers.

steps.title: Rules and formats
steps.body:
- A = L + C; modern rules: assets/expenses Dr ↑; liabilities/capital/income Cr ↑
- BRS: add/subtract by asking 'which record is higher and why?'
- Errors: omission, commission, principle, compensating; suspense for one-sided errors
- SLM (C − S)/n; WDV % × opening BV; profit/loss on sale = price − BV
- Provision on debtors after bad debts
- Final accounts: every adjustment twice
- Partnership default: equal sharing, no interest on capital, no salary, 6% on loans

steps.title: Presentation slips
steps.body:
- Missing narrations
- Not showing working notes
- Wrong side for balance c/d
- Mixing ₹ and thousands

steps.title: Time plan
steps.body: Spend ~1.5 minutes per mark; write working notes beside long questions so partial marks are possible.

cards.back: Deduct from expense; show as current asset

quiz.why: Outstanding salary is salary owed but not yet paid. It is a liability.

quiz.q: Cheque deposited not cleared: passbook vs cash book:
quiz.why: A cheque deposited but not yet cleared is already in the cash book, but the bank hasn't credited it yet. So the passbook balance is lower.
Without a partnership deed, profits are shared equally, under the Partnership Act.
Compensating errors cancel each other out, so the trial balance still agrees. They don't affect agreement.

scenes.text: Nisha maps every cost formula onto one page grouped by question type.
When she reads a question she first finds its box on the map.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Cost sheet: prime → works → COP → COGS → cost of sales → profit
- EOQ √(2AO/C); ROL = max × max; Min = ROL − normal × normal; Max = ROL + ROQ − min × min
- Halsey: TT × R + 50% TS × R; Rowan: TT × R + (TS/TA) × TT × R
- MHR = overheads/machine hours
- BEP = FC/contribution per unit; FC/PV; MOS × PV = profit; PV = Δprofit/Δsales
- MPV (SP − AP)AQ; MUV (SQ − AQ)SP; LRV (SR − AR)AH; LEV (SH − AH)SR

steps.title: Sanity checks

scenes.text: In 1897, Mr Salomon's boot business failed. Creditors argued he and his company were the same person.
The House of Lords disagreed: the company was a separate legal person. That idea underpins all company law.

steps.title: Features of a company
steps.body:
- **Separate legal entity** (Salomon v Salomon & Co Ltd, 1897): the company owns property, sues and is sued in its own name
- **Limited liability** of members (by shares or guarantee)
- **Perpetual succession**: members may change; the company continues
- **Transferability** of shares (restricted in private companies)
- **Lifting the corporate veil**: courts or statute look behind the company for fraud, tax evasion, sham companies, or when it acts as an enemy agent

steps.title: Kinds (Companies Act, 2013)
steps.body:
- **Private company**: restricts share transfer, max 200 members (excluding employee-members), min 2 members and 2 directors
- **Public company**: min 7 members and 3 directors
- **One Person Company (OPC)**: single member (a natural person), min 1 director
- **Small company**: private company within prescribed paid-up capital and turnover limits
- **Section 8 company**: promotes charity, education, art, etc.; profits not distributed
- **Government company**: at least 51% paid-up share capital held by government(s)
- Holding/subsidiary, listed/unlisted, limited by shares/guarantee, unlimited

steps.title: Solved: classify the company
steps.body:
- Four friends, 150 shareholders, shares not freely transferable → **private company**
- A company whose 60% shares are held by the Government of Gujarat → **government company**
- A non-profit set up to run a free library, licensed by the Central Government → **Section 8 company**

steps.title: Solved: lifting the veil
steps.body: A director forms a company only to dodge a non-compete promise he personally made. A court can treat the company as his alter ego and grant relief against both — the veil is lifted because the company is a **sham** to evade a legal obligation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking shareholders own the company's assets directly.
- Saying a private company must have 7 members.
- Confusing limited liability with no liability.
- Treating every company with government shareholding as a government company (it needs ≥ 51%).

steps.title: Incorporation
steps.body:
- Promoters conceive the company and take steps to form it
- Name reservation and incorporation are filed online with the Registrar of Companies (through the MCA portal's integrated incorporation form)
- Documents include the MoA, AoA, declarations and subscriber/director details
- The **certificate of incorporation** is conclusive evidence that the company is incorporated; it carries the Corporate Identity Number (CIN)
- Minimum paid-up capital requirements were removed by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015

steps.title: MoA and AoA
steps.body:
**Memorandum of Association** (charter; defines scope):
- Name clause, registered office clause, objects clause, liability clause, capital clause, and subscription/association clause

**Articles of Association** (internal rules): management, meetings, transfer of shares, directors' powers. Model articles are in Schedule I (e.g. Table F for companies limited by shares).

The MoA prevails over the AoA if they conflict. Alteration generally needs a **special resolution** (some changes also need approval from the Central Government or Tribunal).

steps.title: Solved: ultra vires
steps.body:
**Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co v Riche (1875)**: a company formed to make railway carriages agreed to finance a railway in Belgium. The contract was outside its objects clause and **void ab initio** — even unanimous shareholder approval could not ratify it.

Today: an act ultra vires the MoA is void; an act ultra vires the directors but within the company's powers can be ratified by members.

steps.title: Solved: which clause?
steps.body:
- Moving the registered office from Pune to Bengaluru → **registered office clause** (inter-state shift needs Central Government approval)
- Adding a new line of business → **objects clause**
- Increasing authorised capital → **capital clause** (ordinary resolution, if the articles permit)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking ultra vires contracts can be ratified by shareholders.
- Saying AoA overrides MoA.
- Forgetting that the certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence.
- Believing a minimum ₹1 lakh capital is still needed for private companies.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

story.title: The bank and the borrowing limit

scenes.text: A bank lends to a company on the directors' word. Later the company claims the loan needed a shareholder resolution that was never passed.
Can the bank recover? The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders acting in good faith.

steps.title: Two doctrines
steps.body:
- **Constructive notice**: anyone dealing with a company is presumed to know the contents of its public documents (MoA, AoA) filed with the Registrar
- **Indoor management** (Royal British Bank v Turquand, 1856): outsiders may assume internal procedures have been properly followed; they need not check the company's internal acts

Exceptions to indoor management: the outsider **knew** of the irregularity; **forgery**; **negligence** (no inquiry despite suspicious circumstances); acts that could not be within anyone's authority.

steps.title: Solved: Turquand-type case
steps.body:
AoA allow directors to borrow if authorised by an ordinary resolution. Directors borrow without one.

- Lender knew of the AoA rule (constructive notice) but could assume the resolution was passed (indoor management)
- **Company is bound**, provided the lender acted in good faith

steps.title: Solved: exception
steps.body:
A share certificate bearing a forged signature of the company secretary is relied upon by a buyer.

- Forgery is a nullity — indoor management **does not** protect the buyer against the company (Ruben v Great Fingall Consolidated, 1906)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking constructive notice protects outsiders (it protects the company; indoor management protects outsiders).
- Applying indoor management where the outsider was an insider who knew.
- Ignoring the forgery exception.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: Outsiders are presumed to know the company's MoA and AoA.
Indoor management protects an outsider who knew the required resolution was not passed.
Royal British Bank v Turquand established indoor management.
A forged document can bind the company under indoor management.

quiz.why: The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders dealing in good faith from internal irregularities (Turquand's rule).
Constructive notice means outsiders are deemed to know the contents of public documents, such as the MoA and AoA.

quiz.q: Which is an exception to indoor management?
quiz.why: Forgery is an exception to indoor management, because a forged document is a nullity.

quiz.q: An outsider is put on inquiry when:
quiz.why: An outsider is put on inquiry when the circumstances are suspicious. Then he can't rely on indoor management.
Royal British Bank v Turquand was decided in 1856.

scenes.text: A popular food-delivery company files for an IPO; the newspapers discuss its 'red herring prospectus' and price band.
Company law sets out what the prospectus must contain and who is liable for misstatements.

steps.title: Prospectus
steps.body:
- A **prospectus** invites the public to subscribe for securities; includes shelf prospectus and red herring prospectus (without final price/quantity)
- Misstatements: **civil liability** (Section 35) to compensate investors and **criminal liability** (Section 34) for untrue or misleading statements
- Public issues are also regulated by SEBI regulations

steps.title: Share capital
steps.body:
- Authorised (nominal) → issued → subscribed → called-up → paid-up
- **Equity shares** (voting, residual claim) and **preference shares** (priority for dividend and capital repayment)
- **Securities premium** (Section 52): may be used only for specified purposes, e.g. issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or issue expenses, buy-back
- Shares generally **cannot be issued at a discount** (Section 53), except sweat equity shares (Section 54)
- **Rights issue** (Section 62), **bonus issue** (Section 63)
- **Buy-back** (Section 68): generally up to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves; board approval up to 10%; post-buy-back debt–equity ratio not above 2 : 1

steps.title: Solved: capital structure
steps.body:
Authorised 10,00,000 shares of ₹10; issued 6,00,000; subscribed 5,50,000; ₹8 called; all calls paid except ₹2 on 10,000 shares.

- Authorised capital ₹1,00,00,000
- Subscribed ₹55,00,000
- Called-up ₹44,00,000; calls in arrears ₹20,000
- Paid-up **₹43,80,000**

steps.title: Solved: buy-back limit
steps.body:
Paid-up capital ₹40 crore + free reserves ₹60 crore = ₹100 crore.

- Maximum buy-back with a special resolution = 25% = **₹25 crore** (equity buy-back is also capped at 25% of paid-up equity capital in a year)
- Board alone can approve up to 10% = ₹10 crore

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using securities premium to pay dividends (not permitted).
- Saying shares may freely be issued at a discount.
- Confusing subscribed with paid-up capital.
- Forgetting SEBI rules apply in addition to the Act for listed companies.

steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

quiz.why: Shares can be issued at a discount only as sweat equity shares, which is a statutory exception.

quiz.why: Civil liability for a misstatement in a prospectus is under Section 35 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Bonus issues are under Section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.why: After a buy-back, the debt–equity ratio must not exceed 2 : 1 (the general limit).

questions.why: A company is an artificial legal person: created by law, with its own legal identity.

questions.why: The Memorandum of Association (MoA) is the charter of a company.

questions.why: The member of a One Person Company (OPC) must be a natural person, an individual.

questions.why: Indoor management protects outsiders who deal with the company in good faith.

questions.why: Securities premium may be used for issuing fully paid bonus shares, among other permitted uses (Section 52). It can't be used for salaries or dividends.

questions.why: An ultra vires contract is beyond the company's capacity, so it is void from the start. Even all shareholders can't ratify it. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.why: A government company is one where at least 51% of paid-up capital is held by the Central Government, State Governments, or both.

questions.q: Which may lead courts to lift the corporate veil?
questions.why: Courts may lift the veil when a company is used to evade tax, as this is an abuse of the corporate form.

questions.q: Case: Directors needed a members' resolution to borrow above ₹1 crore (AoA). They borrowed ₹2 crore without it. The lender did not know. Is the company bound?
questions.why: The lender didn't know about the missing members' resolution, which is an internal irregularity. Under the indoor management rule, the company is bound.

questions.q: Paid-up capital ₹50 crore; free reserves ₹30 crore. Maximum buy-back by board resolution alone:
questions.why: A buy-back by board resolution alone is limited to 10% of the paid-up capital plus free reserves. Here that is 10% × (50 + 30) = ₹8 crore.

questions.q: Subscribed 1,00,000 shares of ₹10, ₹7 called, calls in arrears ₹15,000. Paid-up capital:
questions.why: Paid-up capital = amount called and paid. 1,00,000 × ₹7 = 7,00,000 called, less 15,000 in arrears = ₹6,85,000.

options: the company is bound by indoor management
the company is not bound (forgery is a nullity)

When the company defaulted, Kamal learnt that directors have legal duties whether or not they attend.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- Numbers: public company ≥ 3, private ≥ 2, OPC ≥ 1; maximum 15 (more by special resolution) — Section 149
- At least one director must have stayed in India for at least 182 days in the financial year (resident director)
- Listed companies: at least **one-third independent directors**; prescribed companies need at least one **woman director**
- Every director needs a **Director Identification Number (DIN)**
- Maximum **20 directorships**, of which not more than **10 public companies** (Section 165)
- **Duties** (Section 166): act per articles, in good faith for the company, employees, shareholders, community and environment; with due care, skill and diligence; avoid conflicts; no undue gain; no assignment of office

- One-third of 9 = 3 ⇒ it needs **at least 3** independent directors — non-compliant

steps.body:
Meera is a director in 8 public companies and 10 private companies (none dormant, no exclusion applies).

- Total 18 ≤ 20 ✓; public 8 ≤ 10 ✓ ⇒ she may accept **2 more** directorships, and at most 2 of them can be public.

- Counting independent directors as a fixed number rather than a fraction.
- Confusing DIN with PAN or CIN.

scenes.text: A company secretary realises the AGM notice went out only 15 days before the meeting.
The Act requires 21 clear days (unless shorter notice is consented to). She reschedules.

steps.title: General meetings
steps.body:
- **AGM** (Section 96): every company except OPC; first AGM within 9 months of the end of the first financial year; thereafter within 6 months of year end, gap ≤ 15 months
- **EGM** (Section 100): any other general meeting
- **Notice** (Section 101): at least **21 clear days**; shorter notice with consent of prescribed majority
- **Quorum** (Section 103), unless articles require more — public company: 5 members (≤ 1,000 members), 15 (1,000–5,000), 30 (> 5,000); private company: 2
- **Ordinary resolution**: votes in favour > votes against; **special resolution**: votes in favour ≥ **3 times** votes against (Section 114)

steps.title: Board meetings
steps.body:
- First board meeting within **30 days** of incorporation; at least **4** meetings a year with a gap of not more than **120 days** (Section 173)
- Quorum (Section 174): one-third of total strength or 2 directors, whichever is higher

steps.title: Solved: special resolution
steps.body:
At a meeting, 6,300 votes are cast for and 2,000 against a proposal.

- 3 × 2,000 = 6,000 ≤ 6,300 ⇒ **special resolution passed**
- With 2,200 against, 3 × 2,200 = 6,600 > 6,300 ⇒ fails as special but passes as ordinary.

steps.title: Solved: board quorum
steps.body:
Board strength 10.

- One-third = 3.33 → rounded up to **4**; higher than 2 ⇒ quorum = **4 directors**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the day of notice and the meeting day as 'clear days'.
- Thinking OPCs must hold AGMs.
- Applying public-company quorum to private companies.
- Requiring 75% of members present for a special resolution (it is 3 × votes against among those voting).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.
